slides.say: A school has two buses. Bus A carries four times as many students as bus B. Six students move from bus A to bus B. Afterwards, bus B carries half as many students as bus A. How many students are on the two buses altogether?

Students move from one bus to the other, and the ratio changes. We'll solve it two ways, the math way with an equation, and then by understanding, with divisibility, which needs almost no calculation.

Let's start with the math way. Bus A carries four times as many as bus B. Remember, the plain x goes to the smaller one. B is the smaller bus, so B is x and A is four x. No fractions, and no dividing later.
at: so B is x and A is four x

slides.say: Six students move from A to B. A loses six, so A has four x minus six. B gains six, so B has x plus six.
Afterwards, B carries half as many as A. So two times B's new number is equal to A's new number. B has x plus six, and A has four x minus six. So two times x plus six is equal to four x minus six.

Now we open the brackets. So two x plus twelve is equal to four x minus six. We take two x from both sides, and add six to both sides. Twelve plus six is eighteen, so eighteen is two x. Divide both sides by two, and x is nine.

Careful, don't mark nine. That's bus B at the start, and they ask about both buses together. Moving students doesn't change the total, so the total is x plus four x, five x. Five times nine is forty-five. Choice number two is our answer.
at: so the total is x plus four x
Choice number two is our answer

slides.say: Now by understanding. We start again from the givens. At the start, A has four times B. So for every one student on B, there are four on A. One part and four parts, five parts in all. One part is B's number of students, a whole number. So the total is five times that whole number, and is divisible by five.
Forty-eight isn't divisible by five, so choice number three is out.

After the move, B has half of A. So B is one part and A is two parts: three parts in all. One part is again B's whole number of students. So the total is divisible by three. And it's the same total as before, because the students only moved between the buses.

Forty is thirty-nine plus one. And thirty-nine is three times thirteen. So forty isn't divisible by three. Fifty is forty-eight plus two. And forty-eight is three times sixteen. So fifty doesn't either. Choice numbers one and four are out.

Only forty-five is left, and it is divisible by both. Forty-five is five times nine. It's also three times fifteen. For whole numbers of students, use a fully reduced whole-number ratio. The total is divisible by the sum of its parts. Check that condition before and after the move. Choice number two is our answer, and I'll see you in the next question.
at: Choice number two is our answer
